passages.t: The shut gate, and those who may serve
passages.happening:
The man brought Ezekiel back to the outer east gate, ‘but it was shut’ (verse 1). ‘This gate is to remain shut. It shall not be opened, and no man shall enter through it, because the LORD, the God of Israel, has entered through it’ (verse 2). Only the prince may sit inside the gateway to eat before the LORD (verse 3).

At the front of the temple Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD filling the house again, and he fell on his face (verse 4). God charges Israel with bringing foreigners into his sanctuary to serve there. ‘No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh may enter My sanctuary’ (verse 9). The Levites who went astray after idols will bear their guilt; they will guard the gates and serve the people, but they will not come near to serve as priests (verses 10-14).
passages.hearers:
The east gate is shut because the glory has entered by it. It is a picture of God's return being permanent: the way he came in will never again be used as a way out.

Foreigners had served in the temple in earlier days. The Gibeonites were assigned as woodcutters and water carriers, and the royal guard in the temple courts probably included foreign soldiers. Ezekiel treats such practices as a breach of covenant.

The Levites who had served at the shrines of idols are given lesser duties. The priests of Zadok's line, who served in Jerusalem, alone may serve at the altar.
passages.later: Isaiah foresaw foreigners ‘who join themselves to the LORD’ brought to God's holy mountain (Isaiah 56:6-7). The Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers for the altar (Joshua 9:27).
passages.hard:
Doesn't the exclusion of foreigners clash with the Bible's welcome to the nations?

It can sound that way. Isaiah 56 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the LORD will be brought to his holy mountain, and Ezekiel 47:22-23 itself gives resident foreigners an inheritance among the tribes. The key is the phrase uncircumcised in heart and flesh (verse 9). Ezekiel is not excluding people because of ethnicity, but because they were outside the covenant altogether, serving in God's house without belonging to God, often as hired or conscripted workers. His target is Israel's carelessness in letting them.

Some interpreters see a real difference in emphasis between Ezekiel, who stresses purity after the disaster of idolatry, and Isaiah 56, which stresses inclusion. Others see the two as agreeing that access to God's house requires covenant faithfulness. The chapter gives no warrant to shut anyone out of worship because of where they come from.
passages.asks: The gate the glory entered by stays shut. Ask what it means that God has come to stay. And ask what doors in your own life you need to close behind you.

passages.happening:
‘But the Levitical priests, who are descended from Zadok and who kept charge of My sanctuary when the Israelites went astray from Me, are to approach Me to minister before Me’ (verse 15). They are to wear linen when they serve, and change out of it before they go out to the people (verses 17-19). Rules follow for their hair, wine, marriage and mourning (verses 20-27).

‘They are to teach My people the difference between the holy and the common, and show them how to discern between the clean and the unclean’ (verse 23). They will judge disputes and keep God's feasts and Sabbaths (verse 24). ‘In regard to their inheritance, I am their inheritance’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Holiness in the temple was treated almost like a physical force, passed on by contact, which is why the priests change their linen before going among the people. Linen was cool and clean, while wool made the body sweat, and the ideal was a body that produced nothing unclean in God's presence. The rules on hair, wine, marriage and the dead largely echo Leviticus. Ezekiel's marriage rule is stricter than Leviticus for ordinary priests, though it allows marrying a priest's widow.

The priests' work was not only sacrifice. They were to teach and to judge. And they owned no land, because God himself was their portion.
passages.later: God told Aaron, ‘I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites’ (Numbers 18:20). Malachi said, ‘For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge’ (Malachi 2:7).
passages.asks: The priests had no land, because God was their inheritance. Ask what it would mean for God to be enough for you. And ask whom you could help to tell the holy from the common.
